Neonatal hooded seals emerge from parturition at a standard body length of 100 centimeters [Lb = 100 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the substantial in utero growth characteristic of this pagophilic species. Newborn pups, known as "bluebacks" for the bluish-grey pelage they display prior to their first moult, weigh approximately 18,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 18,000 grams] at birth, a mass that positions them among the larger phocid neonates relative to maternal body size. This substantial birth mass is an adaptation to the abbreviated lactation period typical of ice-breeding seals, where rapid mass gain is essential for survival. The dense, insulating lanugo coat provides critical thermal protection on the unstable pack ice of the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans. This neonatal stage is brief but energetically demanding, with pups relying entirely on their mother's lipid-rich milk to fuel a period of accelerated growth. The high fat content of the milk, often exceeding 60 percent, allows for efficient energy transfer from the female to her offspring during the short window of maternal attendance. Consequently, the initial body length of approximately one meter serves as a baseline from which the rapid somatic development of the suckling juvenile phase commences.

The period of maternal investment in Cystophora cristata is remarkably condensed, with weaning occurring only seven days after birth [tx = seven days after birth] under the normal core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] for this species. During this intense nursing interval, the pup undergoes a dramatic transformation in body composition, as the wet weight at weaning reaches approximately 43,300 grams [Wwx = approximately 43,300 grams]. This represents a mass gain of over 140 percent relative to the birth weight, a growth rate that is among the highest recorded for any mammal. The mother fasts throughout the entire lactation period, mobilizing her own blubber reserves to produce the energy-dense milk. The brevity of the suckling stage is an evolutionary response to the unpredictability of the pack ice habitat, where a prolonged dependency period would expose the vulnerable neonate to increased risks of predation by polar bears and anthropogenic disturbance. Following this rapid weaning, the pup is abruptly abandoned on the ice and must transition to nutritional independence, relying on its accumulated fat stores until it learns to forage. This abbreviated nursing phase imposes a severe energetic bottleneck on the juvenile.

Growth continues steadily after the nutritional independence onset, but the attainment of full adult size requires several years. Females reach their ultimate total length of 203 centimeters [Li = 203 centimeters], whereas the larger males exhibit a more extreme maximum length, reaching 260 centimeters [Li = 260 centimeters], a figure that underscores the strong sexual selection operating on male body size in this polygynous phocid. The ultimate wet weight for females plateaus at approximately 300,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 300,000 grams], while males attain a substantially greater adult mass of 405,000 grams [Wwi = 405,000 grams]. This dimorphism is directly linked to the species' mating system, where males engage in intense competition for access to females on the breeding ice. Body size is a primary determinant of success in these contests, selecting for the evolution of larger male body dimensions. The disparity in mass is more extreme than the difference in length, reflecting the greater investment in blubber stores that males must acquire to sustain extended periods of fasting during the breeding season. Females, by contrast, prioritize the efficient transfer of energy to their offspring over maximizing their own somatic bulk beyond the adult plateau.

Reproductive maturation in the hooded seal follows a sex-specific schedule that is closely tied to body condition and resource availability. At a core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], puberty in females, defined as the time since birth at which gonadal maturation is complete, occurs at 1,095 days after birth [tp = 1,095 days after birth]. Males, however, require a considerably longer developmental period, with the age at puberty recorded at 1,826 days after birth [tp = 1,826 days after birth] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delayed male maturation is a common pattern among polygynous pinnipeds, where younger males are physically incapable of competing with older, larger competitors for access to receptive females. The gestation period is also subject to an obligate embryonic diapause, a strategy that synchronizes parturition with favorable ice conditions. The total gestation time, including the period of delayed implantation, spans approximately 240 days [tg = approximately 240 days] at the species' typical core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This prolonged gestation ensures that birth occurs on stable pack ice in late winter or early spring, maximizing neonatal survival.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the hooded seal is calculated at approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] under the physiological conditions sustained by a core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This longevity is modest compared to some other phocid species, such as the bowhead whale or the elephant seal, reflecting the high metabolic demands of an Arctic existence and the substantial energetic costs associated with extreme reproductive investment. Adult females typically produce a single pup per breeding event [N_R_i = single pup per breeding event], a litter size that is invariant across most years, and this breeding event occurs once annually [F_R_i = breeding event occurs once annually], a pattern typical of capital-breeding phocids that must accumulate sufficient blubber reserves to support both gestation and the intense lactation fast. The combination of delayed maturity, small litter size, and extended maternal investment places the hooded seal firmly within a slow life-history strategy, despite the exceptionally rapid rate of neonatal mass gain that characterizes the brief nursing period.
